title: The good warrior
hookLine: the best warrior isn't warlike; the best leader serves below (Tao Te Ching 68)
last: GENTLENESS, ECONOMY, AND NOT DARING TO BE FIRST.

cards: Chapter sixty-eight is short, and it reads like a job description written backwards. Wanted: a soldier who isn't warlike. A fighter who doesn't get angry.
Someone good at winning who doesn't get drawn into the fight. A boss who puts himself underneath everyone he works with. It sounds like a list of people who'd be fired by Friday.
The chapter says these are the skilled ones, and it gives the whole quality a name.

teach.b: First, not warlike, not angry. The one skilled as an officer, the chapter says, is not martial, and the one skilled in fighting doesn't fly into a rage.
Toughness that has to be shown off is easy to spot, and easy to push. And anger, whatever else it does, makes a fighter easy to read.
Second, winning without engaging. The one good at overcoming opponents doesn't get tangled up with them. There's skill in not taking the bait, in letting the provocation pass by.
Third, placing oneself below. The one good at using people puts himself below them: not giving orders from a height, but underneath, like the person holding the ladder while someone else climbs.
That's the line behind today's carry. Fourth, the name.
The chapter calls this the virtue of not contending, and the power of making use of others, and says it matches heaven, the highest standard of the ancients.
Yesterday's three treasures included not daring to be first; some readers see today's warrior as that treasure carried into a fight.
It's the shift lead who refills the supply closet, the parent who sits on the floor to talk at eye level, the team captain who carries the water bottles. Strong enough not to need to look strong.

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching, including students of martial arts and of leadership, take chapter sixty-eight as a portrait of calm strength: no rage, no showing off, and a leader who serves from below.

o: a champion who has never lost a single battle
a fighter who isn't warlike and serves from below
a soldier who fights only for heaven's own cause

s: chapter sixty-eight says the best fighters are the angriest
it says the one skilled in fighting doesn't fly into a rage.
the chapter says the one good at using people puts himself below them
underneath, not over, like someone holding the ladder.
the chapter calls this the virtue of not contending
and says it matches heaven, the highest standard of the ancients.

games.q: someone tries to provoke you into a fight. according to chapter sixty-eight, what does the one good at overcoming opponents do?
o: doesn't get tangled up with them.
games.why: the chapter says the one good at overcoming opponents doesn't engage with them, and calls this the virtue of not contending.

practice: Bring to mind one person you lead, teach, look after, or simply have a little power over, and picture yourself holding the ladder while they climb. What do they need from below: time, a tool, someone to steady things?
Let one answer come, and keep your breath steady, the way a good hand on a ladder stays steady.

wordCard.voice: The good warrior. In chapter sixty-eight, the one who isn't warlike, isn't angry, and puts himself below others. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: not martial, not warlike, from the opening of chapter sixty-eight.

carryVoice: Your line: serve below. The ladder needs a steady hand at the bottom. That's today.
